_notes: CHAPTER 1, COMPLETE (opening arc: owner brief 2026-08-04; back half:
2026-08-08, from chapters/01-case-file-wax-and-wick.md as amended).
The opening arc, in the order the board offers it:
follow_the_thread -- the obvious move, tried first: the thread is CUT
(owner 2026-08-10: 'why does he not just follow
that thread' -- now he does, and the player
chooses which of the two starting jobs to take)
find_the_magpie   -- the Exchange, and gleam being worth something
the_carrying      -- the witches come for her; the Case Board opens
what_i_saw        -- Ash goes back over last night alone (Crossing)
ask_the_rats      -- the Ratsmeet, and how to ask a question (Testimony)
sharpen_the_claws -- growth: he decides to get harder to kill
the_wake          -- her funeral; her last seam, sewn by the player
Then the investigation proper, chained on evidence, not on quest ids:
creditors            -- the counting-house heist; the ledger; BODKIN ENTERS
the_lamplighters_talk-- Merrow's round, her testimony, the hall ward mended
the_ward_that_failed -- the Wickhouse; the backward seam; Remembered Day 1
an_audience_of_wax   -- the Tallowman, Wick's books, the verdict choice
Sides: night_rounds / garden_route / empty_coat (fight-chains with faces),
the_milk_debt (Tansy + the Gentleman's paper), the_pigeon_ballot (the
murder-night seed; needs the docket, so its break is always possible).
Quests are ProwlScript `steps`: fight, story, flashback, minigame, lesson.
Lessons play ONCE (data/lessons.json) and replay from the Casebook. A
story step may gate on `when_minigame` success/loss -- a lost testimony
must never be followed by the page narrating the confession (law 17).
GATING: the_carrying is the only CORE work after the Magpie, because a
body being carried out of your house does not wait its turn. The three
middle jobs open together; the_wake waits for all three; the back half
waits for the_wake and then chains itself on the evidence each lead
yields. Every Bodkin line is LITERALLY TRUE (docs/design/the-unraveler.md
-- read it before giving him a single new word).

follow_the_thread.name: The Thread Itself
follow_the_thread.board_card: One strand of her thread still runs out under the window and into the city. The obvious thing is to follow it. I am going to do the obvious thing.

lines: The strand under the window, still running, still hers. Every other thread in this house was cut clean — nobody cut THIS one.
Magic is needlework: her words, said at the table like a recipe. Witches stitch the world, cats can see the seam. Follow it, then. Paw on the line, like tracking a fly across a window.
The strand under the window again, patient the way only thread is. It did not go anywhere. I did.
Paw on the line. From the top.
It runs the rooftops the way I do — chimney to chimney, never crossing an open street. Whoever holds the far end knows this city the way the city hopes nobody does.
And where it crosses the gutter-line something has found it first, drinking the hum off it the way moths drink a lamp. That is not trespass. That is grave-robbing.
Past the lane the thread drops to street level and runs straight for the Mere — and the fog stands up to meet it, thick as a held breath.
There is no fighting through this. There is only getting across it without losing the line.

on_loss_lines: I come out three streets wrong, with the line lost twice and found twice.
The fog wanted the thread walked away from. Noted, and declined.

lines: At the Mere-edge the thread runs out over the sea-wall and stops. Mid-air. Above the water.
Not frayed, not worn through. CUT — one clean bite, the same as the threads on her walls, by something that could SEE it. Almost nothing can.
So the thread is not a road. It is an answer of its own: whoever did this reads the Weft — the stitching under the world — cuts clean, and did not want to be followed home across the water.
A trail closed on purpose has to be bought open, and the Shambles keeps a fence who knows everyone worth asking. The long way round, then.

find_the_magpie.name: Find the Magpie
find_the_magpie.board_card: A cat with a question and no answers needs a fence. Brindle keeps a stall in the Shambles and keeps everything else besides.

steps.art_desc: The Shambles after hours: stalls shuttered under canvas, one lit fence's stall at the lane's end with a magpie behind it, Ash in his red kerchief walking toward it with a thimble in his mouth
lines: I cannot stay in this room tonight, and the room knows it. The thread runs into the city, and the city sells answers.
Brindle keeps a stall in the Shambles after the market has gone to bed, and nobody talks for nothing. That is the first true thing about Hollowmere.
So I bring payment: her second-best thimble, carried openly in my teeth — you do not walk up to a fence with your payment hidden. Dignity and I will discuss it later.
Down the Shambles again, the thimble back in my teeth. It kept. Dignity did not.
Unfinished work waits. That is the whole of its nature.
Halfway down the Shambles, something comes up out of a drain for the shine in my mouth.
A gutter-wisp — and it is not after ME at all. It wants the thimble: witch's silver, small enough to steal.
Small lies and small valuables. It cannot tell the difference and it has never once needed to.
The drain is loud again — the shine in my mouth rings them up like a bell.
Rooms this cheap never stay empty.

steps.art_desc: Brindle the magpie fence behind a market stall of buttons, teeth and small keys, one bright eye, night market lanterns
lines: I arrive at the stall with the thimble still in my teeth and my dignity somewhere behind me on the cobbles.

Brindle is on her perch above the shutters, black and white with that oil-slick green in the wing, doing the thing magpies do that looks like idleness and is inventory. She speaks before I have set the thimble down.
'You are the witch's cat.' — 'Was,' I say. She does not say sorry, and I like her enormously for it. Sorry is what people say instead of anything useful.
'Back,' says Brindle, before I have said anything at all. Fences know their street; knowing it is the whole trade.
Being remembered in this city is halfway to a friendship — and all the way to a debt.
'Clear the wisps out of my back alley and we can have a conversation like professionals.'
She has not touched the thimble. 'Three nights they have been in my stock, hunting anything with a seal or a shine on it, and I am one bird.'
A fence with a wisp problem. Payment, it turns out, comes in kinds.
'The alley, pet. Three nights of wisps in my stock, and I am one bird. Clear it, then the conversation.' She has not touched the thimble.
'I need to know who was on Needle Lane last night.'
'Right,' says Brindle, when the alley is quiet. 'You're not useless. That's the whole interview.' She takes the thimble at last, and holds it a moment longer than trade requires.
'Bring me buttons and I'll remember harder. Doors open now. Mind the step.'

the_carrying.name: The Carrying
the_carrying.board_card: There are women at the door of the house. They have brought a sheet. This is not something to be attended — it is something to be witnessed.

lines: Three witches came at first light, and nobody sent for them. They did not knock. Witches do not knock at a house where a witch has died; a knock asks a question, and the house has already answered it.
Mother Cardew is the eldest of the Circuit. Small and grey and folded, like something kept a long time at the bottom of the workbasket — and her eyes went round the parlor once, at working speed.

I asked how they knew. 'Nine seats,' said Cardew. 'One rope between the nine of us. A seat goes out, the weight comes onto the rest, and you feel it in your wrists whether you're minding or not.' She had felt it at dusk, with a pan in her hand.
Eight seats, now.
I asked why she waited for morning. 'You don't walk Needle Lane in the dark. Not while something is still —'

steps.art_desc: Three witches in grey lifting a shrouded body from a chair in a cold parlor at dawn, a black cat watching from the mantel
lines: They lifted her the way you lift someone who might wake. That is the thing I will allow them, all three, forever.

Cardew stopped at the door and looked back at forty years of workings hanging cut at one tidy height. 'Who did this to the room,' she says. Not a question — burglars take things, and nothing here was taken.
And then Cardew was looking at me, colleague to colleague, while everyone else looked at the floor.
One chance to be taken seriously. A cat who yowls is comforted. A cat who performs is petted.
choices: Tell her exactly what came in the door.
Say nothing. Watch what she does with silence.
Ask what unpicks a witch's own stitching.
steps.art_desc: The workroom doorway from inside: cut threads hanging the length of the frame, scissors and pinned patterns on the table, cold morning light

lines: I told it, all of it, in order, as she taught me anything worth saying should go. Cardew listened the whole way through without moving.
Then she said, quieter, to nobody: 'Again.' She put the word down like something she had not meant to be holding. AGAIN means BEFORE, and a thing with habits can be found.
I say nothing. Cats are good at nothing; it is most of what we do. She waits me out, which nobody does, then gives up first, which nobody does either.
'It has happened before. Twice that I will admit to.' At the door: 'Mind the room, cat. Rooms hold a while. After that —' She did not finish it.
'What unpicks a witch's own stitching?' I ask. The room gets colder in a way the room is not responsible for.
'Something that learned it from her,' says Cardew. 'Or from one of us.' She looks at her two frightened girls, and does not look at them for quite long enough.

The day-side came at nine. Two constables, not unkind, who tried the window catch and saw an old woman dead in a chair behind a door locked from the inside. 'Heart, most like,' the older one said. 'At her age.'

The younger wrote it down, stepped twice over a thing under the window I had not yet found, and they were gone in ten minutes. I went through everyone whose office this might be, and reached the end twice.
So I minded the room, the way she went over a hem: slowly, twice, against the nap. Under everything, faint, pond-bottom and old rope and patient water — and the Mere does not come up to Thimblefield.

And under the window, the thing the constable stepped over twice: a beeswax stub, burned an inch down, pinched out, stamped with the bee. She burned tallow her whole life and called beeswax the rich man's smell.
Out of that inch of wax I built the man who left it, and what follows is a thing I built, not a thing I found. An inch is an hour, and an hour of lit window on Needle Lane should have been seen.
Then I remembered the shutters, closed for the first time in fifteen years, and thought: of course. He closed them. I was pleased with that.

what_i_saw.name: What I Saw
what_i_saw.board_card: Nobody asked me to do this. I am going to walk that night again, in order, until the order of it gives something up.

lines: A thing I have learned about being the only witness: everyone believes you, and nobody acts on it.
So. From the top: the roof, the market, the lane, the lamps. Not for anybody — for the order of it.
The gutter first, where the wisp came up for my little lie. There is another one in it tonight. There is always another one.
The lamps on Needle Lane are still out. Nobody has been up the ladders — the Lamplighters are not coming, which is itself a fact.
And the fog off the Mere is up over the whole street, lying where fog has no business lying. It lay here that night too, and I had other business. Tonight the fog IS the business.
No claws for this. Across it, corner by corner, reading the lane the whole way.

on_loss_lines: I come out of it four streets wrong and shaking, which is data of a kind.
Whatever is in that fog does not want the lane walked. Noted.

lines: Out the far end, at the mouth of the lane, in the gutter where a wheel would throw it:
A cart docket. Chandlers' paper — the bee in the corner — for a delivery, night of, Needle Lane. And the consignee line filled in by a hand that then thought better of it and scratched it out.
Somebody drove a cart down a street with no lamps on it, at night, and did not want to be the sort of person who had. That takes a professional. That takes a QUIET one.
The long way round, then — streets I know, to the lane's far mouth, arriving like a tourist.
And there, in the gutter where a wheel would throw it: a cart docket. Chandlers' paper — the bee in the corner — night of, Needle Lane, consignee scratched out.
Somebody drove a cart down a dark street and did not want to have. That takes a professional. That takes a QUIET one.

ask_the_rats.name: Ask the Rats
ask_the_rats.board_card: Nothing crosses this city at night without a rat watching it and pricing the information. Brindle says go to the Ratsmeet. Brindle says wear my patience.

lines: The Ratsmeet convenes under the fish market in the hour the ice melts, and every rat in Hollowmere sends somebody.
There is a protocol. You do not eat anybody. You do not say 'trap' or 'terrier'. You do not be a cat about it. (Once. We do not discuss the terrier.)
And you do not argue with the doorman. The doorman is a goose. Rats are not stupid: a goose cannot be bribed, and has never once liked a cat.
Under the fish market again, in the hour the ice melts. The protocol holds, and so does the doorman.
The goose remembers me. The feeling is mutual.

steps.art_desc: The boss of the Ratsmeet: an ancient grey rat on a throne of market crates under a fish market, chalk tallies and ledgers around him
lines: Their boss is grey to the point of transparency. He will tell you he remembers the ninth bell. Nobody argues with him.
'The witch's cat,' he says. 'We had a lively night. Everyone had a lively night.'
He will talk. Rats always talk — for a price, in a shape. While he finishes his ice, I limber up on the doorman.

on_loss_lines: He tells it beautifully and I cannot get a claw into any of it.
'Come back when you know more,' he says, which is the politest possible way to bill me for an hour of rat time.

lines: A cart with no chandler on it, and a gentleman behind it going nowhere in particular. The Grey Boss charges honest rates once he has stopped lying.
You cannot clear out of an empty street. I will be keeping that one.
By morning the Chandlers will know a cat was asking about their cart. Good.
A rat's silence is a price list. He knows the lane's story; the lane knows; I am the only one paying retail.
Still: 'a lively night,' he called it, on a lane he swears was empty. Empty lanes are not lively. I will come back armed.
By morning the Chandlers will know a cat was asking about Needle Lane. Word is the one thing this market gives away free.

sharpen_the_claws.name: Sharpen the Claws
sharpen_the_claws.board_card: The thing in the parlor went through me like I was a curtain. That is not happening a second time. There is a wall behind the tannery that nobody minds about.

lines: Here is the part nobody puts in the stories: I lost.
It came into her house and I did everything I know how to do, and it did not even hurry.
I am fifteen. I had put my working nights away without telling anybody, there being nobody to tell. Whatever I was at eight is not in this body, and I am not going to be given it back.
So I will go and get some of it again, deliberately, too late, and badly. That is still faster than waiting to be improved by events.
First: the Watch goose behind the tannery, which has never lost an argument in its life. That is what makes it worth arguing with.
Elspeth used to say the difference between brave and stupid is about four seconds of looking. Watch it. THEN decide.
Next lesson: the dog at Number Twelve, who has eleven feet of chain, no appointments, and a standing offer to discuss territory.
Slower this time. Watch what the thing in front of you is going to do BEFORE deciding what you are going to do about it.
And one more thing, which is not fighting and is the reason for the fighting.
Her ward is still on the door frame, and it has a hole in it the size of the thing that walked through it.
She patched this door every autumn of my life while complaining about the weather. I have watched it four hundred times. Watching is not the same as doing. I am about to find that out.

on_win_lines: It holds. It is not her work — hers was invisible and mine can be seen from the street — but it holds.
Nothing comes through that door tonight that I have not agreed to.
on_loss_lines: I get most of it and the last corner will not take, and I sit with my nose an inch from the gap until it is light.
Fine. Not tonight, then. Tonight I just watch the door myself.

lines: There is a wall behind the tannery that has been holding up nothing at all for sixty years.

I go at it until my legs are wrong, and then a bit past that, and then I lie down in the dark and listen to my own heart being annoyed with me. In the morning my shoulder will not have come back. Some of it never will.
Better. Not enough. But the kind of not-enough that has a direction in it.

the_wake.name: The Wake
the_wake.board_card: They give her to the tide at the turn of the evening. Every guild will send somebody to be seen not caring, and I am expected to be decorative. She expected better.

steps.art_desc: A witch's funeral at the tideline at dusk: a shrouded figure on a low bier, women in grey, guild delegates at a careful distance, a black cat on a mooring post
lines: The quay was fuller than I expected and emptier than she deserved. The Lamplighters sent four, everyone the hall has left, lamps burning at half-wick. The Magpie sent a bird with one respectful button laid on the stones.
The Chandlers sent one man, early, standing precisely where he could be seen being sorry.
No grave. No fire. Cardew took the bone needle and began sewing the shroud shut in Elspeth's own stitch. Four stitches in, she stopped.
'I don't know her hand,' she said. Quietly. To the linen. 'Sixty years, and I don't know her hand.' Nobody moved, and the seam stood open four stitches.
I have watched those hands from the windowsill all my life. I know the hand better than I know my own name, which she also gave me.
I got up onto the bier. Somebody started forward to stop me, and Cardew said 'Let him,' in a voice that ended the subject for a generation.

on_loss_lines: A cat is not built for needlework. I pushed the bone needle with a paw and drew the thread in my teeth, and the first stitch took me three tries, like the kettle.

The last corner beat me. Cardew finished it without a word about it. She does not say I did well; she puts one small hard hand flat on my back for a moment, which is not a thing witches do to cats they have just met.

lines: The seam closed. The tide took her without discussion — no speeches, no splash, the grey linen going down through the grey water until it was a paleness, and then a memory.
One lamplighter forgot not to salute.

Then Cardew did the thing for which I will forgive her everything else, always. In front of the guild delegates and the roofline and the Chandlers' man in very good black, she bent down. It cost her; I heard her knees pay it.
She tied a small grey knot into the thread at my chest, where the whole Weft could read it. 'A debt,' she said. 'Mine. You'll know.'

Walking me back up the quay, low, for my ears alone: 'It has happened twice before. Both times a stitcher. The Tatterstage's lead player, forty years gone. And Widow Sarn of Hemlock Row, three winters after.'
'Nobody looked, either time. The Circuit closed the files. I signed the closing.' A pause. 'I'm too old to open them again. Too watched, as well.'
I asked who would look now. 'Seven of us, holding what she held, and a thing under this town that wants a hand on it every hour of the night. There's no spare hand in this city to go asking who.'
At the sea-wall: 'You are neither.' A pause. 'You were her ninth, you know. She'd never say what she meant by the count. Find who did this, cat.'
Ninth. I filed the word next to AGAIN, in the drawer of things said to me that were heavier than the sayer knew.
Ninth. I filed it next to 'twice before', in the drawer of things said to me that were heavier than the sayer knew.
Home, to a house with nobody in it. The kettle sat where I left it, off the fire on the cold hearthstone, and it was the wrongest thing in the room — a kettle off the fire is a kettle finished.
My whole job used to be: be somewhere warm at the correct time. All right, then. New job.

creditors.name: Creditors
creditors.board_card: The counting-house keeps paper on everything the Chandlers do. Somebody should read it. Cats cannot be arrested, only despised.

lines: Brindle first, because paper is her native language and mine only by adoption. She reads the flimsy head cocked, one eye at a time: watermark, fold-grease, ink that had been wet in fog.

Then she flicks it flat to take the corner, and stops. Half a second, her working eye on the cart-slot seal. Then she goes on as though the seal were weather, and I was too new to ask what she had not said.
'Counting-house paper. The originals live under the ledgers, second yard off Wick Row. Mind the night shift, pet.'
Brindle again, and shorter this time. 'Second yard off Wick Row, pet, same as it was. The night shift will remember you. Walk like you don't.'
Wickrow after dark is the best-lit district in the city: every doorway a warded bee, burning in its own wax and billed to the tenants by the quarter. Other streets buy locks. Wickrow buys light.
The night shift is a counting-house hound, off its chain. The yard is a box and the box is his — he does not have to catch you, he only has to go on standing between you and the one hole.

Whatever settled that yard, it was not speed; I have none to bring to a hound and have not had for years. But it cost me the quiet — the lantern came round, and I came off the wall into a blind alley-mouth.
A paw hooked my scruff and hauled me through a gap I had not seen, and held me in a doorway's dead shadow while the watch went past.
A grey tom. Old, big-boned, one eye, half an ear, and the stillness of a creature long practised at being exactly as visible as it chooses.
'Watch the paws, not the claws. Claws are a rumor. Paws are an appointment. The dog told you where he would be four moves before he got there, and you were reading the teeth.'
'Wax door, far side. Wick's paper is worth the reading.' — You know what I am looking for, I said. 'I knew your witch to look at,' he says. 'Everyone did.'

At the alley-mouth, the doorway's dead shadow already has its tenant. A paw takes my scruff through the same gap, same silence. Bodkin does not give a lesson twice; he watches me use the first one instead.
Then he gave me one more thing I had not asked for, flat, and worn smooth with saying.

'Nobody collects off a lit candle. You take a house's light, you take its salt, you take its fire: take any of the three and you take nothing else under that roof that night. Not a debt. Not a favor. Not a mouse.'

'It is not manners. Manners you can decline. It is older than the Hollow Court and older than the desk they keep in it.' — 'Bodkin,' he says at the fence, his name given once. It meant nothing to me then.

The wax door keeps its own porter: one of the Chandlers' night staff, poured and lit, standing in the doorway like a votive that took the job seriously. It does not challenge me. It simply fails to move.

on_loss_lines: The ward re-crosses itself faster than I can read it, and somewhere below a bell taps twice, politely.
The counting-house knows a cat is in it. Fine. Cats have been despised by better buildings than this one.

lines: Under the ledgers, the originals, and in them her name. VANE, in a strong small impatient hand: the renderers' tallow debt, two winters' workroom rent, a seven-year chandlery account forgiven in name and never in law.

'Buy it quiet, pay the premium for quiet, and call it due Lady's Day.' Every debt she owed in the world, bought in seven days by one buyer. I made myself read it twice, because the first reading had a red wash over it.
A man who does this is planning an eviction, not a murder. And you particularly do not kill the needle holding shut something you profit by. A dead seamstress mends nothing.
Out over the yards with a page of a rich man's handwriting folded into my shadow. Paper says what Wick WANTED; paper does not say what he DID.
For that I need people who watch the Chandlers for a living and hate them fluently.

the_lamplighters_talk.name: The Lamplighters Talk
the_lamplighters_talk.board_card: The Lamplighters hate the Chandlers professionally. Hate is chatty — and their hall has questions of its own about that night.

steps.art_desc: The Lamplighters' hall by night: empty coats on pegs over boots nobody came back for, a chalk tally board, four lamplighters at one lamp, Ash in his red kerchief at the door
lines: The Lamplighters' hall burns lamps at its own door. That costs a guild that cannot spare the oil: their own light, spent outward at the dark, all night, every night, as a point of order.
I stopped on the wall opposite and read the front of that building like a notice. We are not gone. We light what we have. Come home.

Inside, one cold room. Most of the coats on the pegs hang over boots nobody has come back for — pairs of boots, toes out, waiting, under coats that keep their shapes the way the wraith on Needle Lane kept a shape.
Forty lamplighters used to walk Hollowmere. What is left of the guild fits in that room, around one lamp, with room to spare. It goes quiet when a cat comes in.
The hall again. The talk thins when I come in, and does not stop — which is the hall's way of saying it remembers me. One of the four moves his boots so I can pass.
They knew me the moment I came in. THE WITCH'S CAT went around the room the way words go around a room full of people not saying them, and the room braced.
The one to convince is obvious. Torn ear, chalk on her paws, and a shift-boss's way of standing: facing the door, near the lamp, where the next bad news has to go through her first.
Merrow.
choices: Lay the ledger page on the floor between us.
Ask after their missing, and listen.
Sit. Wait to be spoken to.

lines: Merrow is at the lamp, facing the door. She does not ask why I am back. She waits to see how I will open, this time.
choices: Lay the ledger page on the floor between us.
Ask after their missing, and listen.
Sit. Wait to be spoken to.

lines: The page goes down on the boards. Merrow reads Wick's hand upside down, which tells me she has read it before. Other pages. Other nights.
'Paper,' she says. 'The Chandlers are made of it. Walk my round with me, cat. Rounds first. Paper after.'
I look at the coats over the boots and ask after their missing, which has the advantage of being true. The room stops bracing.

'Not dead,' says Merrow. Flat, fast, a door long since slammed on that word. 'The Court said not dead. Our filings come back MARKED: no appointments under those names. Eleven names, filed again every week.'
'The day-side says contract work up the coast. There is no paper in the world that says where a man is not.' She looks at the pegs. 'Rounds first. Come.'
I sit. I am prepared to be furniture for an hour; furniture usually wins. It takes four minutes — I am the first party to come into that hall and not open with the murder.
'Fine,' says Merrow, taking up her pole. 'You do manners. Walk my round with me and we will see what else you do.'

Her round is forty-one lamps, and something is walking it ahead of us: lamps lit at the head of the round, dark again behind us. Not blown, not failed. DRUNK — wicks wet and whole, the warded bees drained to grease.

At the fifteenth we double back and catch them at it. A pair of wisps working her lamps in sequence, one keeping watch while the other drinks. Appetite does not read route-maps, and it does not keep a schedule.
Merrow plants the pole. 'Get them off my round, cat, and I will believe every next thing you say.'

The round costs me a flank — a fence I would have cleared at eight, and did not quite clear tonight. It bleeds quietly; I say nothing about it and finish the round. She relights her lamps in her order to the round's end.
At the hall door she chalks a fresh tally on the wood, one stroke among hundreds, and I understand that the strokes are rounds completed since the night of the missing.
'You came about the night,' she says. 'Ask, then. I answer what is asked. No more.'
That is a doorway exactly the width of your own wits.

on_loss_lines: Merrow answers exactly what I ask, and I ask it wrong, and the wall of her holds.
'Out of questions?' She is not gloating. She is disappointed, which is worse.

lines: I did not ask who killed her, nor what happened to her missing. I asked what work Elspeth Vane did in Wickrow that nobody paid for. Merrow looked at me like a colleague who has found the fault you walked past.
'That is Wick's hand,' she says, tapping the requisition. 'And that is the night nobody signed.' Two facing pages: two years of Wickhouse ward-shifts, logged, walked, witnessed, and paid to nobody.
Nobody sews free. She least of anyone — I have watched her price a churn-blessing to the ha'penny and then chase the ha'penny.

Questions are not the only tool in a hall full of torn things. Merrow hands me the tally anyway — two years of Wickhouse ward-shifts, paid to nobody — because the tally is her own grievance, and grievances want witnesses.
Nobody sews free. Elspeth least of all. Whatever is in the Wickhouse, she thought it was worth her thread.

Behind the meeting-board their own ward hangs torn — ripped the night of the missing and left that way, because the one who always mended it is one of the coats. They have been living inside a torn ward every night since.
Merrow sees me looking. The whole room sees Merrow seeing. Cats inspect seams, by ancient arrangement, and getting up onto the meeting-board takes me two tries with that flank.

on_win_lines: I mend their ward in front of everybody, better than I did the parlor door, because the parlor door taught me how.
When it is done the hall hums faintly, low, under the talk. One of the four remaining lamplighters puts his face in his hands. Everyone else looks at the lamp.
on_loss_lines: I patch what will take, and the last gap beats me, and Merrow puts her own hand over it without a word.
'First mend this hall has had since the night,' she says. 'Somebody had to be first.'

lines: Merrow walks me to the door. At the threshold, in front of her whole guild, she ties a lamplighter's knot into the thread at my chest — rough work, honest, tight.
'The hall owes the cat,' she says, for the room.
And then, bending close, for me alone, in the voice she keeps for the end of bad shifts: 'Wisps do not learn a route. Somebody taught them the taste. Find the teacher.'
The Wickhouse next. Her last work is holding a rich man's dark shut, and I want to know what it is holding it shut ON.

the_ward_that_failed.name: The Ward That Failed
the_ward_that_failed.board_card: The Wickhouse ward is Elspeth's stitching, kept for free on a warehouse full of dark. Go read her last work. Bring nothing that burns.

lines: The Wickhouse squats on the Mere-edge, fat as a tick, warded to the chimneys in her stitch. You can smell the wax three streets off. Under the wax: the water.
Bodkin is on the sea-wall like he grew there, sitting where he can see the water. 'You are going to the Wickhouse.' It is not a question.
'Nothing good ever came off that water. Keep your feet dry and your business short — and go in by the wax door, not the water door.' He stays on the stone. 'I don't go in there.'

on_loss_lines: The fog rearranges the streets while I am inside them, and I arrive wet to the elbows and short a card or two.
The Mere got a taste. It will remember me. Ledger that under: mutual.

lines: At the wax door, the fog has residents. One of them is between me and the handle, dry-footed on a wet street.
It is not fast. It does not need to be fast. It is ARRIVING, the way the tide arrives, and the door behind it is the one I need.
The seam is thin out here — I can feel her stitching through the wall, holding. Whatever the Drowned want, it is inside.
In by the wax door. Wax to the rafters — white hills of it, a hundred winters of light not yet sold.

And under the merchant smell, the other one: pond-bottom, old rope, patience — the smell that had no business in her parlor. Something lives at the water end of this warehouse, and the wax is not stock. The wax is FEED.
Her seam runs the length of the water wall, stitch after stitch after stitch. Fifteen years I watched her leave at odd hours with her kit. Here is where the hours went.

on_loss_lines: I read her seam the way a kitten reads: out loud, slowly, losing the thread of the thread.
But I keep her count, and the count is the part that matters. The seam and I understand each other now.

steps.title: The Ninth Stray
lines: Her table, years ago. This same chart, half-sewn, and a much smaller cat deployed on top of it as a paperweight.
'Eight I tried, over the years,' she tells the needle, not me. 'Not one of them stayed long enough to finish. The ninth fell asleep on my work, and I took it for a signature.'
She sews around me rather than move me. Count, hook, count, mirror at the turn. I know her hand the way you know weather.
I never once thought to ask what the seam was FOR, or what she meant by the count — Cardew's question now, as well as mine.
Back in the cold warehouse, her seam in front of me — and it is wrong at the near end. Not torn. Not burned. UNDONE: each stitch lifted out clean, in her own hand, in her own order.
Her order, run BACKWARD. To read what was done here, I have to sew it the way it was unsewn: her stitch, mirrored, back to front.

on_loss_lines: Backward defeats me tonight. It should defeat anybody.
That is the point. I will be thinking about that all the way home.

lines: A hand's length of her thread comes away with the reading — the piece the unpicker lifted and left hanging. Hers, then mine.
The ward did not fail. It was UNPICKED: her exact stitch, mirror-handed, faster than any needle honestly goes. I thought those words once already, standing at her chair.
Cardew said it, in her parlor: something that learned it from her — or from one of us. Learned without being taught, then. A different crime, with a shorter list of suspects. I do not like how short.
Perfect technique, and Elspeth taught exactly nobody. So something learned her hand without being taught — a different crime, with a shorter list of suspects. I do not like how short.
Out by the wax door. Bodkin is gone from the sea-wall; the fog holds his shape for a second, and then does not.
The wax feeds a thing the guild will not name, her ward holds it, she held the ward unpaid — and the man who profits from the holding bought her debts. Four facts, one knot.

an_audience_of_wax.name: An Audience of Wax
an_audience_of_wax.board_card: Guildmaster Wick will see you now. Everyone in Wickrow is suddenly very polite. Mind the big one.

lines: A candle arrives at my door. Beeswax, bee seal, wick trimmed to burn exactly one hour: a Chandlers' invitation. You light it and start walking, and if it dies before you arrive, so does the appointment.
The first free Chandlers' light this house has ever seen, offered to the cat. I carry it lit through the streets in my teeth, like a comet with dignity problems, and Wickrow is suddenly VERY polite.
A second candle arrives, trimmed to the hour, no note. The Chandlers do not run out of wax, or of patience.
I carry it lit through the streets, and Wickrow is polite all over again.
The Guildhall is a chapel to the bee: ten thousand votives, all lit, the heat of them standing in the room like a body.
Between me and the stairs the votives' keeper unfolds — a tower of poured wax with a gentle face and hands like warming pans. 'The Guildmaster will see you,' it says kindly, 'presently.'
Up the stairs, past the puddle with opinions, into the office: Ellery Wick, small behind a desk built to make everything else smaller, already talking.
'You have questions. Everyone has questions. Ask me anything — you will find I have nothing at all to hide.' Which is what that sentence is always for.
So I put it all on his desk. The stub. The ledger page. The tally. The length of unpicked thread. Item by item, in the order a case is told.

The books come out and the books are TRUE, which is the awful part: he bought her debts to buy her BUILDING. The Wickhouse thing is dying, the wax is its last diet, and her free wardwork was ruining the price of fear.
'I wanted her EVICTED,' he says, and his voice does its first honest thing all evening: it shakes. 'Evicted, and alive somewhere cheaper. So who ELSE knew the ward was hers?'

Then he shows me the thing he has been sitting on since the night: the counterfoil for his own cart-slot, signed out for Needle Lane against FAVOR-paper. A debt the Chandlers owed, called in blind. No name asked.
'It came through the usual quiet channels. One does not ask. The not-asking is what the quiet costs.' Wick is guilty of everything except the murder. Cross him off.
He watches me decide what to do with him, which is the most honest fear in the room.
A guild that sells the dark. A warehouse full of teeth. A dead woman's unpaid thread. And a guildmaster who would very much like this conversation to stay between us.
choices: Expose him. The city reads his books at eight bells.
Squeeze him. Take a guildmaster's knot instead.

lines: By eight bells the Lamplighters have his books and by nine the criers do. Merrow reads the ward-shift page aloud on the hall steps. Twice. The second time slower.
Wick keeps his desk, barely, and hates me with the pure focus of a man who now NEEDS me. Useful, hate like that: a man who hates you carefully never pretends to be out.
'Once,' he says, when he sees what I want instead. A Guildmaster's knot goes into my thread, tied by a man who has never visibly owed anyone anything, hating every loop of it.
Overnight the Chandlers become exquisitely civil to one particular cat. Civility, from a guild, is an invoice.
Home. The board gets its last pin of the season: a counterfoil, and a thread running from it to a gentleman nobody meets. Favor-paper drains toward Gravamen, where the carts change hands.
One suspect off the board. One name-that-is-not-a-name waiting on it. The kettle stays quiet, and so, tonight, do I.

night_rounds.name: Night Rounds
night_rounds.board_card: The streets don't watch themselves. Someone ought to be paid for this. Someone is not.

lines: The lamps are short-handed and the dark has noticed. Somebody ought to walk the streets that miss their light.
Nobody hires a cat for this. But a burst wisp spills every shine it ever drank, and the gutter does not ask for it back — the work pays itself, in small change.
First stop: the corner gutter, which is glowing.
Two more down the lane, sharing one appetite between them. Wisps used to be rare on this street.
Used to be.
Last leg, past Number Twelve, where the dog and I keep a standing appointment neither of us has ever missed.

garden_route.name: The Garden Route
garden_route.board_card: Cross the back gardens. Wake nothing. The dahlias are not the danger.

lines: Six gardens between the Shambles and Thimblefield, and the fastest way through all of them is a gate nobody has opened since the old captain died.
It is not locked. It is WOVEN — withies through withies, and whoever did it knew what they were doing.

on_loss_lines: It tightens on me twice and I go over the wall like an amateur, which costs me a claw and all of my composure.
Somebody good made that gate. I would like to meet them and I would like to not.

lines: The gate un-weaves without a whisper. Which leaves the Watch: a goose in the first garden with nothing to do all night but listen.
You cannot unpick a goose. Some things simply have to be argued with.
The gate fought loud, and the first garden heard it: the Watch goose is up, and delighted about it.
Quiet was the plan. The plan has been amended.
Past the goose: the captain's lawn, and the Captain. The chain of office is load-bearing, and the bird underneath it is worse.

empty_coat.name: An Empty Coat
empty_coat.board_card: A coat on Needle Lane is out wearing someone's evening. Object to this.

lines: There it is, halfway up the lane, keeping the height of a man. A Lamplighter's coat, by the cord on the shoulder.
One of the eleven, then — the names Merrow files every week, and every week the filings come back marked NO APPOINTMENT. Not dead. Somewhere.
One of the missing, then — the hall sent four to her wake, everyone it has left, and this coat is not one of the four. A coat only walks for the missing. Not dead. Somewhere.
The wisps have found it first — two of them, drinking the lie of a man who is not there.
The coat has noticed me objecting. It straightens — the way he must have straightened, clocking on.
The coat remembers the shape of him. Now so do I.
The coat comes quiet in the end. I walk it back to the hall and leave it on its peg, over its boots, toes out, waiting.
Fenn takes it off me at the door — the steadiest round of the four they have left — and hangs it himself, and squares the boots under it, and says nothing.
Nobody says anything. Everybody sees.

the_milk_debt.name: The Milk Debt
the_milk_debt.board_card: A kitten sold her purr to the Quiet Gentleman. The Court of Whiskers considers this Everyone's Problem. Attendance is not optional.

lines: The Court of Whiskers convenes on the ropewalk roof at the wrong hour, on purpose, so that attending is itself a sacrifice.

The docket tonight is small, orange, and asleep on the evidence: Tansy, of the canal litter, who sold her purr to the Quiet Gentleman for the favor that fished her brothers out. Contract's legal. Purr's gone.
The kitten wakes up, locates me, and announces to the Court that her counsel has arrived. I have issued no such appointment. The Court minutes it anyway.
'He never signs anything that can be settled,' warns the Clowder-mother. 'Read it before you touch it.' Sound advice for contracts, and for him.
His paper lodges where it always lodges: a strongroom under the Shambles that smells of sealing-wax and of absolutely nothing else. No guards. His paper guards itself.

There it is. Her purr, in escrow: a knot of thread on a shelf, purring faintly to itself. And the knot has grown a loop nobody tied. INTEREST — and a debt owed to itself has its own loose end, which makes it my kind of paper.

on_loss_lines: The knot tightens twice, and I stop before it swallows the loose end. His work does not break. It COLLECTS.
Not tonight, then. Tonight I sit with the little knot and let it purr at me, and we both pretend that helps.

lines: The purr comes loose like a cork and goes home the way purrs do: all at once, at volume, from somewhere behind the ribs. Tansy vibrates so hard she falls off the shelf.
On the shelf where the knot sat: a calling card. Blank, and smelling faintly of fog. It was not there when I started. I do not touch it.
I come back the next night, and the next. On the third the knot gives: cork, purr, kitten, volume. Some jobs are won by arithmetic and stubbornness. Most jobs, honestly.
On the shelf where the knot sat: a calling card. Blank, and smelling faintly of fog. It was not there on the first night. I do not touch it.
Tansy follows me home. I explain that I live alone. She agrees enthusiastically, and moves in. She has decided she is my apprentice. I was not consulted. I begin to see how her contracts happen.
The Court of Whiskers settles counsel's fee at dawn: small shine, counted to the button. Cats keep accounts too.
Somewhere tonight a page of the Gentleman's is one line lighter — and I intend to be a great deal more expensive before he and I are done.

the_pigeon_ballot.name: The Pigeon Ballot
the_pigeon_ballot.board_card: The pigeons are holding an election. Somebody is stuffing the ballot. The ballot is a hat. I wish any part of that were a joke.

lines: The Pigeon Post is electing a Postmaster, which happens twice a century and is decided by hat: you perch on the brim of your candidate, and the hat that bows lowest wins.
A slick young cock called Toby is winning on cleaner ledges and unlimited seed. The seed is real, and pigeons do not ask where seed comes from.
First, the seed itself: it comes up to the roosts from somewhere, in quantity, carried high and scattered wide.
Follow the trail without being seen following it. Pigeons notice a cat on a roofline the way bankers notice fire.

on_loss_lines: Halfway along a ridgeline the whole flock lifts at once, and I flatten into a chimney's shadow and count the feathers going over.
They know something crossed tonight. They do not know it was me. Half a win. The long way up, then.

lines: The trail ends above Needle Lane: a grain-chute, swept clean, the sweepings arranged a little too neatly to be spillage.

Good seed, bought in bulk, hauled UP. Nobody hauls seed up — seed lives at street level, with the spills and the honest pigeons. This was scattered from above, wide as weather, by somebody with HANDS.
The Perch convenes at moonrise to crown the hat. Time the Post heard what its quiet cost — from the one bird whose pride will not survive lying once the paper is out.

on_loss_lines: The Postmaster out-dignifies me in front of the entire Perch, which I did not know was possible and will be studying.
The count stands. But forty pigeons heard the word 'docket', and pigeons repeat things. Give it a week.

lines: 'We voted with our beaks full, and we called the quiet weather.' From a Postmaster, before the whole Perch, that is not gossip. That is a confession with plumage.
So the murder night had a QUARTERMASTER: somebody fed the city's gossip until it slept, days ahead, with human hands and quiet money. The board's quiet gentleman just grew a supply line.
No confession tonight. But the seed came before the night — scattered wide, from above, by hands. Whoever quieted the pigeons planned my witch's murder the way a clerk plans a shipment.
The Perch will finish this without me. Pride is slower than evidence, but it files the same report in the end.
Below, a lamplighter relights Needle Lane, and the first pigeon since the night settles over her old window and says something rude about me. Good. The city is talking again.
Quiet can be bought. Noted, priced, filed. The next time a street goes silent around me, I will know I am standing in somebody's purchase.

the_fish_giver.name: The Fish-Giver Is Late
the_fish_giver.board_card: Pell the Fish-Giver has missed two dawns. Cats don't worry. I am not worried. I am investigating.

lines: Every dawn for eleven years, Pell has set out scraps behind his stall for half the strays in Thimblefield. He calls all of us puss and has never learned one name.
He has now missed two dawns, and the half is assembling on his roof like a jury. Cats do not worry. I am investigating, which is different, and has better posture.
The trouble is on his door, in paper: rent behind, lease called, seven days. The lease runs through a bank, and the bank — I read the seal twice — banks for the Chandlers.
Nobody is going to knife Pell in his parlor. They are going to FILE him out of it. He cannot fight paper and neither can I, but the day-side can be moved by other things.

on_loss_lines: A cat on the roofline at breakfast is conspicuous, and half the street's laundry knows me now.
I get where I am going all the same. Slower. Politer. Watched by sheets.

lines: First asset: the drainpipe behind his stall, and the thing he lost down it nine years ago — his grandmother's brooch, the one he still tells customers about when the fish is slow. No hand fits that pipe. A paw does.
It costs me a wet shoulder, a spider's whole opinion of me, and one bent whisker. I leave it on his counting-slab where he cannot miss it.
Second asset: the pigeons, who owe this street and know where everyone drinks. The landlord's man takes his evenings at the Bent Anchor, loudly, and has a magistrate for a sister.
Third asset: the magistrate keeps a cat, and the cat owes me — a fish-hook, two winters back, extracted without commentary. I sit on her windowsill at dusk and pay the slow blink, and the debt moves.
Dawn, three days later. The shutter goes up. The scraps go down. The jury disperses into a congregation, and Pell stands in the middle of it grinning at nothing, wearing his grandmother on his coat.
In my saucer, under the scraps: a polished scatter of shine. He calls all of us puss; he knows exactly which puss.
'Mind the water, puss,' he says, to all of us, the way he says it every dawn. Somebody once put a saucer down for a stray who had nothing to trade for it. The account stays open.
